To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) participants are able to use a strategy from a simulated physical system as a basis for solving a problem in a completely different domain; (b) performance on the transfer tasks was not related to explicit knowledge of correspondences between the two systems; and (c) performance on the two transfer tasks was not significantly correlated.

(a) people can transfer strategies learned in interaction with a simulated system to an analogous task, and (b) they can do so even when they have no explicit knowledge of the relevant structural correspondences.

(a) people can learn to solve problems in one domain by interacting with a concrete system that simulates that domain, and (b) this knowledge is transferable to a dissimilar problem in a different domain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how people can learn and use abstract representations in the absence of explicit, conscious access to their structure.
the relationship between concrete and abstract information.
the relationship between concrete and abstract representations, and how that relationship affects the ability to transfer strategies learned in one domain to another.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the concrete content of a problem can interfere with transfer, but that it is not necessarily always the case.
the concrete content of two situations is a necessary but not sufficient condition for analogical transfer between them.
analogical transfer between dissimilar systems is facilitated if the systems are perceptually concrete.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ability to transfer strategies learned from one domain to another depends on the degree to which the two domains are perceptually grounded.
we find that people who are better at interacting with physical systems also tend to be better at solving abstract problems.

the ability to spontaneously recognize the structural correspondences in a situation is a critical skill for analogical reasoning, and that the ability to recognize those correspondences may be improved by direct interaction with the system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people can learn to solve problems in a new domain by interacting with a concrete system, and that this knowledge can be transferred to a different, more abstract domain.
people are able to transfer from interacting with a simulated system, even when they have no explicit knowledge of the underlying structure of the system.
the ability to learn from interaction with a concrete physical system may be more general than we have previously thought.
